beats.caption: My baby is here. He is crying. I am exhausted.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths

beats.caption: Everyone says to sleep when he sleeps. Apparently that is also when I’m supposed to do everything else.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths

beats.caption: Same baby. Same income. Same need for food. Now watch our lives split: in one, I get WIC. In the other, I never do.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths

beats.caption: A friend checks in.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Is that food stamps?
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: My friend explains WIC.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Thank God she said something. WIC could help me buy food while I’m breastfeeding—and help feed him as he grows.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: In my other life, that text never comes. I know about food stamps. We have Medicaid. WIC never comes up.
beats.speaker: Without WIC · Maya

beats.caption: I call the number to apply. Before my appointment, I need to gather a few things. First: my ID.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Then my address and Medicaid information. Medicaid helps establish income eligibility. It doesn’t enroll me in WIC.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Now the appointment. Doing it by phone saves a trip, but I still need a stretch of time when I can talk.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: I’m approved. While I’m fully breastfeeding, my package includes $52 a month for produce, plus other foods. Okay. That would help.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Meanwhile, I’m buying the same kinds of food without that help. All of it comes out of my own budget.
beats.speaker: Without WIC · Maya

title: From one person to the country

beats.caption: One text helped me get through the door. But my story is only one of millions.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: Across the country, WIC reaches about 56 of every 100 eligible people. The others qualify for help they aren’t receiving.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: And the chance of getting that help changes depending on where you live.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: In 2023, WIC reached 79.6% of eligible people in Vermont, 62.4% in New York, and 41.3% in Louisiana.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: Those differences don’t tell us why people miss out. They do show that making help available is only the beginning.
beats.speaker: A wider view

title: A place to use the card

beats.caption: Back in my kitchen, the list is getting longer. Being approved is one thing. Now I need a store where I can use the card.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: This run from Keene Valley to Lake Placid is 21.5 miles each way. Now add the baby, the bags, and getting home again.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: I can shop wherever works for me. But at the register, I’ll have to cover the whole bill.
beats.speaker: Without WIC · Maya

beats.caption: This isn’t just one long drive. Nationally, 40% of low-income families with young children live beyond convenient access to a WIC store.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: For a family in a city, that means going more than a mile. In the countryside, more than ten. Having a card doesn’t make the trip disappear.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: At last, the store. I start with the foods on my WIC list: eggs, milk, peanut butter, fruit, and vegetables.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Eggs—but the carton has eighteen. I need dozen-size cartons. Back down the aisle to swap them.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: I don’t have that list to follow. I’m checking prices instead, putting things back when the total gets too high.
beats.speaker: Without WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Fresh fruit for now. Frozen vegetables for later. Those use my produce dollars; the milk and eggs use separate quantities.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: The card will help pay for this food. Getting the right things into the cart is still work. Finally, I head to checkout.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: I’m stocking up on the foods WIC helps me buy. Two dozen eggs, bananas, and carrots go down the belt first.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Then peanut butter and three gallons of milk. The sizes match my benefits this time.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Apples and grapes. I’m buying enough to keep fruit in the kitchen for a while.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Broccoli and spinach for the freezer. Fresh and frozen produce together use $32.62 of my $52 allowance.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: The pasta sauce and white rice aren’t covered. I decide to pay for those myself.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: For this $49.84 shop, WIC pays $46.10. I pay $3.74. That leaves more of my own money for everything else.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: The very same food would cost me $49.84 out of pocket. Without WIC, I have to decide what stays in the cart.
beats.speaker: Without WIC · Maya

beats.caption: At home, the groceries are the part that matters. Some months I make the trip and use the help.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: My groceries run out, too. But there’s no benefit balance to check—just what’s left in my bank account.
beats.speaker: Without WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Other months, I still have benefits when they expire. I meant to go back. Then something else happened.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: The gap between the card and the kitchen shows up in research, too. In this study, substantial produce benefits went unused in about three out of ten certification periods.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: Another month ends. Then another. In both lives, the next big date on the calendar is his first birthday.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths

beats.caption: One candle. A whole year of feeding him. In the life with WIC, another deadline arrives with the birthday.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths

beats.caption: It’s time to renew. The appointment conflicts with work. I put the reminder aside.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Tomorrow, I remember after the office closes. Then I have to check which documents need updating.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: I’m not deciding we don’t need the food. I’m deciding whether I can deal with one more thing today.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: This time, I call before the deadline. I find an appointment I can manage. We stay enrolled.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths

beats.caption: He’s two. His appetite is growing. So are the grocery lists.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths

beats.caption: He’s three. I know which foods work for us. But keeping WIC still means keeping up with appointments.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: He’s four. His need for food hasn’t expired with the paperwork.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths

beats.caption: I’ve kept coming back. How many families manage that? Researchers followed children who enrolled in 2013: fewer than half participated consistently through four and a half years.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: A newer national snapshot looks at separate age groups. WIC reaches 82.3% of eligible infants, but just 26.9% of eligible four-year-olds.
beats.speaker: A wider view

title: What staying can add up to

beats.caption: So what is there to keep? Start with just the produce: up to $52 a month while I’m fully breastfeeding.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: A full year at that rate makes up to $624 for fruit and vegetables.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: From his first birthday, the child’s allowance is $26 a month. One year adds $312.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Another year. Another $312 in produce benefits available to use.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: And another. Small monthly amounts are becoming years of help.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: At the same rates all the way through, that’s up to $1,872 in produce benefits by his fifth birthday. Using them is what turns that number into food.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

title: What all that work is for

beats.caption: Those groceries add up. But do they change what children eat? Researchers looked beyond the bill, scoring the whole diet on a 100-point scale.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: At age three, children who stayed in WIC into their third year scored 3.6 points higher than children who only received it in year one.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: That’s a modest difference in overall diet quality, associated with staying connected to WIC. The years after infancy matter, too.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: Back to Maya. The same fifth birthday in both lives. Five years of needing food—and two different experiences of paying for it.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: Look back at everything it took. WIC made nutritious food more affordable. But the help depended on hearing about it, enrolling, reaching a store, finding the right foods, and managing to renew.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths

beats.caption: More families could benefit if getting started came with a direct referral, staying enrolled fit around work and caregiving, and shopping meant nearby stores, clear labels, and checkout support. Each is a place to remove some of the work.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths

beats.caption: Getting help should take less work.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths
